title: Fashion Finishing & Quality Control
subtitle: Finish hems, collars, closures, linings and details to boutique standard, and prove it with a written quality check before every handover.
description: The difference between a garment that looks homemade and one that looks bought from a boutique is almost always in the finishing. This hands-on course teaches the construction techniques behind clean hems, crisp collars and cuffs, hidden zips, secure closures, well-fitted linings and lasting decorative details, then gives you a written inspection, correction and handover system you can use on every order.

Construct flat and stand collars, plackets, cuffs and waistbands that lie flat and match
Install invisible, lapped and centred zips and sew buttons, buttonholes and hooks that last
Line garments with the right ease and add piping, binding and embellishment that stay secure
Inspect a garment against a 12-point checklist and spec sheet, trace faults to their cause and correct them

modules.title: Professional Hems: Choosing, Levelling and Sewing Them
modules.overview: The hem is the first thing a client sees when a garment moves. In this module you learn to choose the right hem for the fabric and style, level it accurately on the body, sew an invisible hand blind hem, and use machine hems that are fast enough for batch orders without looking cheap.

lessons.title: Choosing the right hem for the fabric, the curve and the client
objectives: Name six common hem types and describe how each one looks from the right side
Match a hem type to fabric weight, hem shape and garment purpose
Calculate a suitable hem allowance for straight, A-line and circle hems
Explain why bias-cut and circle skirts must hang before hemming

blocks.text: A **hem** is the finished lower edge of a garment, sleeve or trouser leg. The raw edge is folded, covered or bound and then stitched so it cannot fray. A good hem does three jobs at once: it stops fraying, it adds a little weight so the garment hangs well, and it gives a clean line that the eye reads as quality. A poor hem, wavy, uneven or showing stitches where it should not, makes even a beautiful fabric look homemade.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.alt: A simple dress with a straight hem
blocks.caption: Every hem decision starts with three questions: what fabric, what shape of edge, and how formal the garment is.

blocks.text: How the curve of the edge changes your choice

A straight hem can take a deep allowance because the folded part is exactly the same length as the garment it lies against. A curved hem cannot. On an A-line or flared skirt, the raw edge is longer than the place it folds up to, so a deep hem forms ripples and little pleats inside. The more curved the edge, the narrower the hem must be.

items: **Straight trousers and pencil skirts:** about 3 to 5 cm allowance, finished with a blind hem.
**Gently A-line skirts and dresses:** about 2 to 3 cm, and ease the extra fullness with a row of long machine stitches pulled up slightly before you press.
**Full circle or strongly flared skirts:** 1 cm or less, as a narrow double fold, a rolled hem, or a facing.
**Shirts with a curved shirt-tail hem:** a narrow double fold of about 0.6 to 1 cm so it turns smoothly around the curves.

blocks.title: Let bias and circle skirts drop
blocks.text: Fabric cut on the bias (at an angle to the threads) stretches under its own weight. Hang any circle skirt or bias-cut dress on a hanger or dress form for at least 24 hours before you level the hem. If you hem it straight away, the hem will dip unevenly a week later when the client wears it.
Matching the hem to the purpose

Think about how the garment will be used. A lady's office trousers need an invisible hem, because visible stitching looks casual. A child's school shirt needs a strong topstitched hem, because it will be washed often and pulled hard. A chiffon blouse cannot hold the weight of a deep fold, so it needs a rolled hem that is light and fine. Traditional styles also have expectations: a buba sleeve or wrapper edge in ankara is often topstitched, while a lace or aso-oke occasion skirt usually needs a cleaner, hidden or faced finish.

blocks.title: Choosing a hem in four questions
items: Fabric weight and transparency
Shape of the hem edge
Formal or casual garment
Speed and quantity needed
blocks.caption: Answer the four questions in order and the right hem type usually becomes obvious.

blocks.title: Worked example: three garments, three hems
blocks.context: For example, Kemi in Ibadan has three orders in one week: navy crepe office trousers, a chiffon peplum blouse, and a wide ankara circle skirt with a 120 cm hem circumference at the waist line and much more at the hem.
steps: Trousers: medium crepe, straight edge, formal. She chooses a hand blind hem with a 4 cm allowance, finishing the raw edge first with overlocking.
Blouse: sheer chiffon, slightly curved peplum edge, light. She chooses a narrow rolled hem with her rolled hem foot, about 3 mm finished.
Circle skirt: ankara, full circle. She hangs it for 24 hours, levels it, trims to a 1.5 cm allowance and sews a narrow double fold (0.5 cm then 1 cm) topstitched close to the inner fold.
She records each choice on the order card so the same client gets the same finish next time.
blocks.result: Each garment gets a hem that suits its fabric and shape, and none shows ripples, heavy folds or visible stitches where they would look wrong.

blocks.text: A quick test before you cut away fabric

items: Fold up the planned allowance on a short section and pin it.
Look from the right side in daylight: is there a ridge, ripple or shadow?
Hold the section up and let it hang: does it fall smoothly or kick out?
If it ripples, reduce the allowance or switch to a facing. Only then trim.

blocks.text: Write your choice down. Professional workrooms keep a simple record of which hem was used on which fabric. Over a few months this becomes your own house standard, and it saves you from guessing every time a client brings a new fabric.

takeaways: Choose a hem by fabric weight, edge shape, formality and quantity
Straight edges can take deep hems; curved edges need narrow hems or facings
Hang bias and circle skirts at least 24 hours before levelling
Test a short section before trimming the allowance

activity.title: Build a hem decision card
steps: List five garments you have sewn or seen recently, with their fabric and hem shape.
For each, write the hem type you would choose and the allowance in centimetres.
Fold and pin a 15 cm test section of one curved hem at two different allowances.
Photograph both from the right side and note which one lies smoothly.

lessons.title: Levelling a hem on the body and sewing an invisible hand blind hem
objectives: Mark a level hem from the floor with the client wearing her own shoes
Prepare the raw edge and hem allowance before stitching
Sew a hand blind hem that cannot be seen from the right side
Press a finished hem without leaving ridges or shine

blocks.text: Most hems that look crooked are not badly stitched. They were **badly marked**. Bodies are not symmetrical: one hip may be higher, the tummy or seat may lift the front or back, and shoes change everything. That is why a professional never measures the hem down from the waist. She measures **up from the floor**, with the client standing naturally in the shoes she will wear with the garment.

blocks.name: straight-ruler
blocks.caption: A firm ruler held upright from the floor is the simplest tool for marking a level hem.

blocks.text: Marking the hem level from the floor

items: Ask the client to wear the garment, the correct underwear and the exact shoes. Ask her to stand straight with her weight on both feet, looking ahead, not down.
Agree the finished length at the front first, for example 4 cm below the knee, and measure that distance from the floor with a ruler held upright.
Use the same floor measurement all round. Mark with pins or tailor's chalk every 5 to 8 cm, moving yourself around her, not asking her to turn.
Check the side seams hang straight down. If a side seam swings forward or back, fix the fit first; a hem cannot hide a fitting problem.
Take the garment off, lay it flat and true the pin line into a smooth curve, joining the marks with a ruler or curve.

blocks.title: No client present?
blocks.text: For a trouser hem without the client, measure the length on a pair of her trousers that she likes, along the inside leg seam. Ask her to confirm by voice note or photo which shoes she will wear, because flat sandals and 8 cm heels need very different lengths.
Preparing the allowance

Once the fold line is marked, measure the allowance below it, for example 4 cm for trousers, and trim evenly. Then **finish the raw edge**: overlock it, zigzag it, or cover it with a light bias binding (called a Hong Kong finish when the binding wraps the edge). On thin fabrics you can turn the edge under by 0.5 cm instead. Fold the hem up along the marked line and press the **fold only**, not the top edge, using the tip of the iron. Pin or tack (baste) with long hand stitches about 1 cm below the finished edge.
The hand blind hem stitch

Use a fine hand needle (a size 9 or 10 sharp is common) and a single strand of polyester or cotton thread in a shade that matches the outer fabric, or is one shade darker. Cut about 50 cm of thread: longer pieces tangle. Run the thread through beeswax or a thread conditioner if it knots easily.

items: Fold the finished edge of the hem back towards you by about 0.5 cm, so you are looking at the inside of the fold and the garment layer just above it.
Hide the knot inside the hem allowance.
Working from right to left (left to right if you are left-handed), pick up **one or two threads only** from the garment layer with the needle tip.
Move along about 0.8 to 1 cm and take a small stitch through the hem allowance only.
Repeat, keeping the thread relaxed. Tight thread will pull dimples on the outside.
Every 10 cm, turn the garment over and check the right side. If you can see stitches, take smaller bites.
Finish with two small back stitches in the allowance and bury the tail.

blocks.title: The blind hem rhythm
items: Catch 1 to 2 threads
Move 0.8 to 1 cm
Stitch hem allowance
Check right side
blocks.caption: Repeat this small loop all the way round and check the right side every 10 cm.

blocks.title: Worked example: hemming office trousers
blocks.context: For example, Bisi in Abuja is shortening new crepe trousers for a client who wears 5 cm block heels to work. The client wants the hem to just touch the top of the shoe at the front.
steps: With the client in her heels, Bisi measures 9 cm from the floor at the front crease and marks with pins. She uses the same 9 cm at the back and both sides.
She checks the old length: the trousers were 7 cm too long, so the new fold line is 7 cm above the old one.
She adds a 4 cm allowance below the new fold line and cuts off the remaining 3 cm, then overlocks the raw edge.
She presses the fold, tacks it, and sews a hand blind hem with stitches 1 cm apart. Each leg has a hem circumference of about 44 cm, so about 44 stitches per leg.
She removes the tacking, then presses with a damp press cloth from the inside.
blocks.result: The trousers are 7 cm shorter, the hems are level in heels and no stitches show from the outside.

blocks.text: Pressing the finished hem

Press from the **wrong side** with a press cloth (a plain cotton cloth or clean handkerchief). Lower the iron, press, lift and move; do not slide the iron along the hem or it will stretch. To avoid a ridge where the top of the allowance sits, slip a strip of brown paper or card between the allowance and the garment while pressing. On dark crepe, wool blends and polyester, too much heat or direct pressing leaves a shine that is difficult to remove, so always test heat on a scrap first.

blocks.title: Iron safety
blocks.text: Keep the iron on its heel when not in use, never leave it on while you step away, and keep the cord out of walkways and away from children. Unplug it at the end of the session. If power surges are common, plug the iron into a surge protector rather than a loose extension.

takeaways: Mark hems up from the floor, with the client in her own shoes
Finish the raw edge before you stitch the hem
A blind hem catches only 1 or 2 threads of the outer fabric
Press hems from the inside with a press cloth and a paper strip

lessons.title: Machine hems for speed: blind hem foot, rolled hem foot, twin needle and overlocker
objectives: Set up a machine blind hem with the correct fold and stitch
Sew a narrow rolled hem on light fabric with a rolled hem foot
Hem knit fabrics with a twin needle or overlocker so the hem can stretch
Estimate time saved by machine hems on a batch order

blocks.text: When you have twenty aso-ebi skirts or a school uniform order to deliver, hand hemming every piece is not realistic. Machine hems can look just as professional, as long as each technique is matched to the right fabric and the machine is set up carefully. The secret is preparation: a well-pressed fold, the right foot, the right needle and a test on a scrap of the same fabric.

blocks.text: 1. Machine blind hem

Most domestic machines have a **blind hem stitch**: a few straight stitches followed by one sideways bite. With a **blind hem foot**, the straight stitches run on the hem allowance and the bite just catches the fold of the garment.

items: Finish the raw edge and press the hem up to its full depth.
Fold the garment back on itself so that about 0.5 cm of the finished edge sticks out beyond the fold.
Place the fold against the guide on the blind hem foot.
Test on scrap: the side bite should just catch one or two threads of the fold. Adjust the stitch width or guide until the bite is tiny.
Sew slowly, keeping the fold against the guide. Unfold and press from the wrong side.

blocks.text: 2. Narrow rolled hem with a rolled hem foot

A rolled hem foot has a small curl at the front that turns the raw edge over twice as you sew. Start by folding and stitching the first 2 to 3 cm by hand-guiding, then feed the edge into the curl. Hold the fabric slightly to the left and lift it a little, so the right amount of fabric enters the scroll. Trim the edge straight and clean first: frayed threads jam the foot. Practise on three or four scraps before touching the real garment.
3. Twin needle hems for knits

Knits stretch, and a single straight stitch on a knit hem will snap when the garment is pulled on. A **twin needle** (two needles on one shank, often 4 mm apart) sews two parallel lines on top with a zigzag-like bobbin thread underneath that can stretch. Use a stretch twin needle, a little longer stitch (about 3 mm) and, if your fabric tunnels into a ridge between the rows, loosen the upper tension slightly or place a strip of light water-soluble or tear-away stabiliser under the hem.
4. Overlocked and turned hem

For casual knits and many quick wovens, overlock the raw edge with a 3-thread or 4-thread overlocker, fold it up once by 1.5 to 2 cm and topstitch, or use the twin needle. On a coverstitch machine, the overlock step is not needed: the coverstitch looper covers the raw edge inside, giving the hem you see on bought T-shirts.

blocks.title: Hand blind hem or machine hem?
items: Hand blind hem
Machine hem
right: Visible dots or lines on some fabrics
Needs the right foot and setting
blocks.caption: Choose by the garment and the order size, not by habit.

blocks.title: Worked example: time saved on an aso-ebi order
blocks.context: For example, Halima in Kano has 24 identical A-line skirts in cotton sateen to hem for a wedding group. Each hem is about 180 cm round. By hand, she sews about 30 cm of blind hem in 5 minutes.
steps: Hand hemming time per skirt: 180 cm divided by 30 cm is 6 sections, and 6 sections at 5 minutes each is 30 minutes.
For 24 skirts: 24 times 30 minutes is 720 minutes, which is 12 hours.
With a machine blind hem after pressing, she times one skirt at about 8 minutes including the test and pressing.
For 24 skirts: 24 times 8 minutes is 192 minutes, about 3 hours 12 minutes.
Time saved: 720 minus 192 is 528 minutes, almost 9 hours.
blocks.result: The machine blind hem saves Halima almost 9 working hours on this order, time she can use to finish and press the skirts properly.

blocks.title: Always test on the real fabric
blocks.text: Thread colour, stitch bite and tension behave differently on every fabric. Sew a 20 cm test on a scrap from the same piece, check it from the right side in daylight and wash it once if the order is large. Fixing a setting on a scrap takes minutes; unpicking 24 hems takes a day.

Keep your test pieces. Label each with the fabric, needle, stitch length and tension you used. A small folder of labelled samples becomes your own reference library, so the next time a client brings sateen or jersey you already know the setting that works.

takeaways: Machine hems are professional when the fold, foot and needle are right
The blind hem bite must catch only one or two threads of the fold
Knits need a stretch finish: twin needle, coverstitch or stretch stitch
Test every setting on a scrap of the real fabric before a batch

quiz.q: A client brings a full circle skirt in ankara and wants it hemmed today. What should you do first?
options: Sew a 5 cm blind hem straight away
Hang the skirt for at least 24 hours so the bias sections can drop, then level it
Cut 5 cm off all round and topstitch
Measure the length down from the waistband at the side seams only
quiz.explain: Bias sections of a circle skirt stretch under their own weight. Hanging first prevents an uneven hem later. A deep 5 cm hem would also ripple on such a strong curve.

quiz.q: Why do professionals mark hems by measuring up from the floor?
options: Because it is quicker than measuring from the waist
Because bodies are not symmetrical and shoes change the length, so the floor gives a level line
Because the waistband is always crooked
quiz.explain: Hips, tummy and seat lift the garment differently. Measuring up from the floor in the right shoes gives a hem that looks level when worn.

quiz.q: When sewing a hand blind hem, you see small dimples on the right side. What is the most likely fix?
options: Take bigger bites of the outer fabric
Take smaller bites (1 or 2 threads) and keep the thread relaxed
Press harder with a hot iron
quiz.explain: Dimples come from catching too much fabric or pulling the thread too tight. Small bites and relaxed thread keep the hem invisible.

quiz.q: Which hem is most suitable for a jersey T-shirt dress?
options: Straight stitch double fold at 1.5 mm
quiz.explain: Knits stretch, so the hem must stretch too. A twin needle or coverstitch hem stretches; a single straight stitch would snap.

quiz.q: Halima hand hems 30 cm in 5 minutes. How long will a 150 cm hem take by hand?
quiz.explain: 150 divided by 30 is 5 sections. 5 sections times 5 minutes is 25 minutes.

quiz.q: A pressed hem on dark polyester crepe has a shiny line. What should she have done?
options: Pressed from the wrong side with a press cloth and a paper strip, after testing the heat
Used a hotter iron for less time
Slid the iron quickly along the hem
Pressed from the right side without steam
quiz.explain: Pressing from the wrong side through a cloth, with a paper strip under the allowance and a tested heat, avoids shine and ridges.

modules.title: Collars, Cuffs and Waistbands That Sit Crisp and Flat
modules.overview: Collars, cuffs and waistbands sit close to the face, hands and waist, so clients notice every bump. This module teaches the construction skills behind a crisp finish: choosing and fusing interfacing, trimming and grading seams, understitching, and attaching each piece so it lies flat and matches its partner.

lessons.title: Flat collars that roll under: Peter Pan and sailor collars
objectives: Choose and fuse interfacing correctly for a flat collar
Trim, grade and notch a curved collar seam so it turns smoothly
Create a slight roll so the under collar never shows from outside
Attach a flat collar with a facing or bias strip so the neckline lies flat

blocks.text: A **flat collar** lies almost flat on the bodice instead of standing up around the neck. The **Peter Pan collar** has rounded ends at the front; the **sailor collar** is square at the back and comes to a V at the front. Both are popular on girls' dresses, school uniforms, blouses and some church and occasion wear. They look simple, but they show every fault: lumpy curves, an under collar peeping out at the edge, and two halves that do not match.

blocks.name: t-shirt
blocks.alt: A top with a neat collar
blocks.caption: Clients look at the neckline first, so the collar must be smooth, symmetrical and flat.

blocks.text: Interfacing: the hidden layer

**Interfacing** is an extra layer that gives a collar body. Fusible interfacing has glue dots on one side that melt onto the fabric when pressed. Sew-in interfacing is stitched in and suits fabrics that cannot take heat or glue, such as some lace, sequinned fabric and very fine silk. For a flat collar, choose a light to medium interfacing: it should be a little lighter than the fashion fabric, because the collar should bend softly, not stand stiff.

items: Test-fuse a small square on a scrap first. Look for bubbles, shine, a stiff feel or glue showing on the right side.
Cut the interfacing from the collar pattern, then trim off about 1 to 1.5 cm at the seam allowance edges so the seams are less bulky.
Place the glue side on the wrong side of the **upper collar** (the one that will be seen).
Press, do not slide. Follow the manufacturer's instructions: many fusibles need about 10 to 15 seconds of firm pressure with steam or a damp press cloth in each position.
Let it cool flat before you move it. The glue sets as it cools.

blocks.text: Making the roll: the under collar is a little smaller

A fabric that folds over itself loses a little length on the outside of the fold. Tailors call this the **turn of cloth**. To make sure the seam rolls slightly underneath where nobody can see it, trim about 2 to 3 mm off the outer curved edge of the **under collar** before sewing (more for thick fabrics). When you pin the two layers together, match the edges: the upper collar will bubble slightly, and that extra is exactly what lets the seam roll under.
Sewing, trimming and turning

items: Pin upper and under collar right sides together and sew the outer edge only, at the seam allowance on your pattern, usually 1 cm for collars.
**Grade** the seam: trim the under collar allowance to about 3 mm and the upper collar allowance to about 6 mm. The layers step down so no hard ridge forms.
**Notch** the outward curves: cut small V-shapes every 1 to 1.5 cm, close to but not through the stitching, so the fabric can fold without bulk.
**Understitch**: press the seam allowances towards the under collar and stitch through the under collar and allowances, 2 to 3 mm from the seam. Stop about 2 cm from each end.
Turn right side out, roll the seam gently between your fingers so it sits just under the edge, and press from the under collar side.

blocks.title: Five steps to a flat collar edge
items: Interface upper collar
Trim under collar slightly
Sew, grade and notch
Understitch to under collar
Roll and press
blocks.caption: Each step removes a little bulk or pulls the seam under, so the finished edge lies flat.

blocks.text: Attaching the collar to the neckline

Tack the two neck edges of the collar together inside the seam allowance so they behave as one layer. Pin the collar to the right side of the bodice neckline, matching centre front, centre back and shoulder seams. On a Peter Pan collar the two halves should meet exactly at centre front, or with the same small gap on each side. Then enclose the neckline with a **facing** or a **bias strip**. A bias strip is quicker for children's wear: sew it over the collar, trim and clip the neck seam every 1 cm, turn the strip to the inside and stitch it down. Understitch facings so they never roll out.

blocks.title: Worked example: matching Peter Pan collar ends
blocks.context: For example, Adaobi in Owerri is making ten school pinafore blouses. The first sample has one collar end 6 cm wide and the other 5.3 cm wide at centre front.
steps: She measures both ends again on the paper pattern: both are 6 cm, so the pattern is correct.
She checks her cut pieces: one under collar was cut 0.4 cm smaller than the pattern, and her seam drifted by about 0.3 cm on the curve.
Total difference: 0.4 cm plus 0.3 cm is 0.7 cm, which matches 6 minus 5.3.
For the batch she traces the stitching line onto each collar with chalk and a template, and sews on the line instead of guessing.
She checks every collar against the template before attaching it.
blocks.result: All ten collars measure 6 cm at each end, within 2 mm of each other, and the halves look identical.

blocks.title: Make a stitching template
blocks.text: Cut the collar shape without seam allowances from thin card or an old file folder. Draw round it on the wrong side of each interfaced collar and sew on that line. Curves come out identical every time, which matters most when the same style is made for a group.

takeaways: Interface the upper collar with a slightly lighter weight than the fabric
Trim the under collar 2 to 3 mm smaller so the seam rolls under
Grade, notch and understitch to remove bulk
Use a stitching template so both collar ends match

Sew, grade, notch and understitch, then turn and press.

lessons.title: Mandarin stands and shirt collars with a band
objectives: Construct a mandarin stand collar that stands up evenly all round
Sew sharp, matching shirt collar points
Attach a collar band so the neckline seam is fully enclosed
Diagnose common stand collar faults and fix them

blocks.text: Stand collars are everywhere in Nigerian fashion: the **mandarin** or **Nehru** stand on senator wear and kaftans, and the classic **shirt collar** with a separate band underneath on office shirts. A stand collar must stand up evenly, meet neatly at the front and never wrinkle at the back neck. A shirt collar must have two sharp points of exactly the same length.

blocks.name: necktie
blocks.alt: A necktie under a shirt collar
blocks.caption: A shirt collar has to hold its shape around the neck, with or without a tie.

blocks.text: Mandarin stand collar

items: Interface the outer stand with a firm fusible. A stand needs more support than a flat collar because it must hold itself upright.
Press the neck edge seam allowance of the **inner** stand to the wrong side, for example 1 cm, before you start. This makes the last step easy.
Sew the outer and inner stands right sides together along the top edge and ends. Grade, notch the curves at the front, turn and press.

Sew the outer stand to the garment neckline, right sides together, matching centre back, shoulder points and the ends to the centre front marks. Clip the garment neckline every 1 cm, not through the stitching.
Press the seam up into the stand. Bring the pressed edge of the inner stand down to just cover the seam line.
Either slip-stitch it by hand or **stitch in the ditch** from the right side so it catches the inner stand underneath. Then topstitch the edges if the style needs it.

blocks.title: Do not stretch the neckline
blocks.text: A curved neckline is partly on the bias and stretches easily. Staystitch it (a line of stitches just inside the seam line) as soon as the pieces are cut, and handle it flat. A stretched neckline is the most common reason a stand collar is too short or wrinkles at the back.
Shirt collar with band

A shirt collar has two parts: the **collar** (the fold-down part with points) and the **band** (a narrow stand that attaches to the neckline and carries the top button). You make the collar first, then sandwich it between the two band pieces.

items: Interface the upper collar and the outer band. Many shirtmakers use a firm shirting interfacing for both.

Sew the collar pieces along the outer edge and ends. At each point, shorten your stitch and take **one or two stitches across the point** instead of pivoting at a sharp angle. This leaves room for the seam allowance inside and gives a sharper point.
Trim the point diagonally, then taper the allowances away from the point. Turn, and push the point out gently with a point turner, never with sharp scissors.
Topstitch the collar edge if required, for example 6 mm from the edge.
Sandwich the collar between the outer and inner band, right sides of the band facing the collar, and sew the band curves and top edge.
Attach the band to the neckline in the same way as a mandarin stand, then topstitch the band all round.

Interfaced band
Garment neckline
Staystitched seam line
blocks.caption: Each layer depends on the one below: a stretched neckline spoils the band and the collar above it.

head: Fault you see
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Stand flops or leans outwards
Interfacing too light
Use a firmer interfacing on the outer stand next time; for now, a second layer on the inner stand can help
Ripples at the back neck
Neckline stretched while sewing
Unpick the back section, ease the neckline back to size with a gathering thread and resew
Collar points different lengths
Uneven stitching at the points
Mark points with a template and sew on the line
Lump where the band ends meet the front
Ends not aligned with the placket edges
Mark centre front on band and placket before sewing and match exactly

blocks.title: Worked example: band length check before sewing
blocks.context: For example, Funmi in Port Harcourt is sewing a senator top with a mandarin collar for a client whose neck measures 40 cm. The pattern stand is 42 cm long between the centre front marks, including 2 cm ease, plus 1 cm seam allowance at each end.
steps: She measures the sewn garment neckline along the seam line, from centre front to centre front: it is 43.2 cm.
The stand is 42 cm, so the neckline is 1.2 cm too long. This means it stretched during handling.
She runs a line of long stitches just inside the seam allowance and pulls it up gently until the neckline measures 42 cm, spreading the ease mostly over the back and shoulder area.
She steams the eased neckline flat and attaches the stand.
blocks.result: The stand fits the neckline exactly, there are no ripples at the back, and the ends meet the front edges cleanly.

blocks.text: On senator and kaftan styles the stand is often topstitched 2 to 6 mm from the edge in matching or contrast thread. Choose one distance and keep it the same on the collar, the front placket and the cuffs, because uneven topstitching distances are noticed straight away on plain fabrics.

takeaways: Stand collars need firmer interfacing than flat collars
Staystitch necklines and measure them before attaching a collar
One or two stitches across a collar point make it sharper
A shirt collar is built in two parts: collar first, then band

activity.title: Stand collar sample and check
steps: Cut a 20 cm wide curved neckline sample and staystitch it.
Make and attach a mandarin stand using stitch in the ditch to finish.
Measure the neckline and stand before attaching and write both numbers down.
Photograph the finished stand from the front and inside.
activity.evidence: Photos of the stand sample with the before-attaching measurements noted

lessons.title: Sleeve plackets and cuffs that match and close neatly
objectives: Sew a continuous bound placket at a sleeve opening
Calculate cuff length from a wrist measurement
Attach a cuff so both cuffs match in width and finish
Place buttons and buttonholes on cuffs in the right direction

blocks.text: A long-sleeved shirt or blouse has an opening at the wrist so the hand can pass through, and a **cuff** that closes the sleeve around the wrist. The opening is finished with a **placket**. Two types are common: the **continuous bound placket**, a single strip that wraps the slit, used on blouses and many dresses; and the **tower placket**, a shaped piece with a point at the top, used on men's and formal shirts. This lesson teaches the continuous bound placket in detail, because it is the one most small workrooms use daily.

blocks.name: coat
blocks.caption: Cuffs are always seen as a pair, so they must match in width, shape and button position.

blocks.text: Continuous bound placket

items: Mark the slit on the back half of the sleeve hem, usually about 7 to 10 cm long, on the line shown in your pattern.
Staystitch a narrow V around the slit line: about 6 mm apart at the hem, coming to a point at the top. Use a short stitch at the point. Cut the slit to the point, not through the stitches.
Cut a strip on the straight grain, about 3 cm wide and twice the slit length plus 2 cm. Press one long edge under by 6 mm.

Spread the slit open into a straight line and sew the strip to it, right sides together, keeping the staystitching just inside the seam allowance. At the point, only a few threads of seam allowance are caught: go slowly.
Fold the strip over to the inside and stitch the pressed edge just over the first seam line.
Fold the front side of the placket to the inside and stitch a small diagonal at the top so it stays inside. The back side stays extended as an underlap.

blocks.text: Working out the cuff size

A cuff must slide comfortably over the wrist bone and allow a watch, but not hang loose. A practical formula is: **cuff length = wrist measurement + ease + overlap + two seam allowances**. Ease for a fitted shirt cuff is often about 3 to 5 cm. The overlap (where the buttonhole end lies over the button end) is often 2 to 2.5 cm. Cuff height for a standard shirt is often about 5 to 7 cm finished.

blocks.title: Worked example: cuff and sleeve gathering
blocks.context: For example, Esther in Jos is making a blouse for a client with a 16 cm wrist. The sleeve hem measures 32 cm around, and she wants a 6 cm deep finished cuff with 1 cm seam allowances.
steps: Finished cuff length: wrist 16 cm plus ease 4 cm plus overlap 2 cm equals 22 cm.
Cut cuff length: 22 cm plus 1 cm plus 1 cm equals 24 cm.
Cut cuff height: the cuff folds in half, so 6 cm times 2 plus 1 cm plus 1 cm equals 14 cm.
The cuff (without the overlap) closes over 20 cm of sleeve, but the sleeve hem is 32 cm, so 12 cm must be eased or gathered in.
She puts two rows of long gathering stitches on the sleeve hem and puts most of the fullness towards the back of the sleeve, where the elbow bends.
blocks.result: Each cuff is cut 24 cm by 14 cm, both sleeves are gathered from 32 cm to 20 cm, and both cuffs come out identical.

blocks.text: Attaching the cuff

items: Interface the outer half of the cuff. Press the free long edge of the inner half under by the seam allowance.
Fold the cuff right sides together and sew the two short ends. Trim, clip the corners, turn and press.
Pin the outer cuff to the right side of the sleeve: one end flush with the front placket edge, the other end extended by the overlap on the underlap side. Sew.
Bring the pressed edge of the inner cuff over the seam and edge-stitch or slip-stitch it in place.
Topstitch all round if the style needs it, then add the buttonhole and button.

blocks.title: Cuff pair check before handover
items: Same finished width
Same finished height
Buttonholes same position
Plackets lie flat
Gathers evenly spread
blocks.caption: Lay the two cuffs side by side and check each point; cuffs are judged as a pair.

blocks.title: Which way do the buttons go?
blocks.text: By custom, women's garments usually close right over left, so the buttonholes are on the right front. On cuffs, the buttonhole goes on the end that laps on top, usually the front edge of the cuff, and the buttonhole runs horizontally along the cuff. Always copy the client's sample or the pattern markings if they differ.

Before you finish, try the cuff closed around your own wrist or the client's. It should allow one or two fingers inside. If it is too tight, it is much easier to move the button now than to remake the cuff later. Some makers sew two buttons a little apart on the underlap so the client can choose a tighter or looser setting, which is a small touch clients appreciate.

takeaways: A continuous bound placket wraps a slit with one straight strip
Cuff length = wrist + ease + overlap + seam allowances
Put most sleeve gathers towards the back where the elbow bends
Check both cuffs as a pair before handover

steps: Measure your own wrist and write it down.
Calculate a finished and a cut cuff size using 4 cm ease, 2 cm overlap and 1 cm seam allowances.
Sew one continuous bound placket on a scrap sleeve shape.
Photograph the placket from inside and outside, with your calculation.
activity.evidence: Cuff calculation sheet and two photos of your placket sample

lessons.title: Waistbands: interfaced, elasticated and faced waistlines
objectives: Calculate the cut length of a straight interfaced waistband
Sew an elastic waistband that does not twist or roll
Finish a faced waistline that stays inside the garment
Choose the right waist finish for a skirt or trouser style

blocks.text: The waist finish carries the weight of the whole skirt or trousers. It must stay flat, not stretch out, not roll over, and be comfortable for a full day of sitting and moving. There are three main finishes: a **straight interfaced waistband** for fitted styles with a zip, an **elastic waistband** for pull-on styles, and a **faced waistline** where there is no visible band at all.

blocks.name: jeans
blocks.alt: A pair of jeans with a waistband
blocks.caption: A waistband carries the weight of the garment, so it needs firm, stable construction.

blocks.text: 1. Straight interfaced waistband

Cut length = **waist measurement + ease + underlap + two seam allowances**. Waistband ease is small, often 1 to 2 cm, because the band should sit snugly. The **underlap** is the extension that sits under the top layer at the zip, usually about 3 to 4 cm, carrying the button or hook. Interface the whole band with a firm fusible, or use a ready-made waistband interfacing with pre-marked fold lines.

blocks.title: Worked example: cutting a skirt waistband
blocks.context: For example, Grace in Benin City is making a pencil skirt for a client with a 76 cm waist. She wants a 3.5 cm finished band with 1.5 cm seam allowances and a 3 cm underlap.
steps: Finished length: 76 cm waist plus 1.5 cm ease plus 3 cm underlap equals 80.5 cm.
Cut length: 80.5 cm plus 1.5 cm plus 1.5 cm equals 83.5 cm.
Cut width: 3.5 cm times 2 (the band folds in half) plus 1.5 cm plus 1.5 cm equals 10 cm.
She checks the skirt waist seam line measures 77.5 cm (76 plus 1.5 ease) after darts are sewn, so it fits the band without stretching.
She interfaces the band, marks centre back and side seams on it, and matches these marks to the skirt.
blocks.result: The band is cut 83.5 cm by 10 cm, fits the skirt exactly and finishes at 3.5 cm high with a 3 cm underlap for the hook.

items: Sew the interfaced side of the band to the right side of the skirt, matching the marks.
Press the seam up into the band. Press under the free edge of the inside band.
Fold the band right sides together at each end and sew across the ends; trim and turn.
Bring the inside edge just over the seam and stitch in the ditch from the right side, or slip-stitch by hand.
Add a hook and bar or a buttonhole and button on the underlap.

blocks.text: 2. Elastic waistband

Elastic waists are common on children's wear, casual skirts and pull-on trousers. Cut the elastic shorter than the waist: a common starting point is about 85 to 90 percent of the waist measurement, but elastics differ in stretch, so **always test** by wrapping it around the body, stretching it over the hips, and checking it is comfortable. Make the channel (casing) about 0.5 to 1 cm wider than the elastic so it can move without twisting.

items: Overlap the elastic ends by 2 cm and zigzag them in a square or box so they cannot pull apart.
After threading, stitch in the ditch through the casing and elastic at the side seams so the elastic cannot twist inside.
For wide elastic (3 cm and more), a few rows of stitching through the elastic, stretching as you sew, give a ready-to-wear look.

blocks.text: 3. Faced waistline

A faced waist has no band. A shaped **facing** follows the curve of the waist on the inside. It is interfaced, sewn to the waist, trimmed, clipped and **understitched**, then tacked to the darts, side seams and zip tape. Understitching is essential: without it the facing rolls out and shows. Some makers stitch a narrow cotton tape or the selvedge of lining along the seam line to stop the waist stretching.

blocks.title: Which waist finish?
items: Faced waistline
Interfaced waistband
Elastic in casing
Elastic plus drawstring
blocks.caption: Fitted, dressy garments suit faced or banded waists; relaxed, everyday ones suit elastic.

blocks.title: Comfort test
blocks.text: Ask the client to sit down during the fitting. A waist that feels fine standing can dig in when sitting. One finger should slide inside a fitted band comfortably while seated.
Common waist faults and quick fixes

head: What you see
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Band wrinkles or buckles when worn
Interfacing too soft, or band cut off grain
Recut the band on the lengthwise grain with firm interfacing
Band too loose after a day of wear
Band stretched while sewing, or waist seam not staystitched
Staystitch the waist and match band marks before sewing
Elastic waist rolls over
Casing too wide for the elastic
Make the casing only 0.5 to 1 cm wider than the elastic, or stitch rows through it
Facing peeps out at the top edge
No understitching, or facing not tacked down
Understitch and tack the facing to darts, seams and zip tape

blocks.text: Whatever finish you use, mark centre front, centre back and side seams on both the band and the garment before sewing. Matching marks is what keeps side seams straight under the arms and stops the band twisting towards one side.

takeaways: Waistband cut length = waist + ease + underlap + seam allowances
Test elastic on the body; do not rely on a fixed percentage
Stitch in the ditch at side seams to stop elastic twisting
Understitch every facing so it stays inside

quiz.q: Why is the under collar trimmed 2 to 3 mm smaller than the upper collar?
options: So the seam rolls slightly underneath and the under collar does not show
So the collar stands up higher
quiz.explain: This allows for the turn of cloth. The upper collar has a little extra, so the seam rolls under the edge and stays hidden.

quiz.q: A mandarin collar ripples at the back neck. What is the most likely cause?
options: The thread was the wrong colour
The stand was cut on straight grain
quiz.explain: Curved necklines stretch easily. A stretched neckline is longer than the stand and ripples. Staystitch and measure before attaching.

quiz.q: A client has a 15 cm wrist. Using 4 cm ease, 2 cm overlap and 1 cm seam allowances, what is the cut cuff length?
quiz.explain: 15 + 4 + 2 = 21 cm finished, plus 1 + 1 cm seam allowances = 23 cm cut.

quiz.q: How do you get a sharp shirt collar point?
options: Pivot exactly at the point and push it out with scissors
Take one or two short stitches across the point, trim, then turn with a point turner
Leave the full seam allowance at the point
Press the point from the right side without turning it fully
quiz.explain: Stitches across the point leave room for the allowance inside, trimming removes bulk, and a point turner pushes it out safely.

quiz.q: A skirt waist measures 70 cm. With 1.5 cm ease, 3 cm underlap and 1.5 cm seam allowances, what is the cut waistband length?
quiz.explain: 70 + 1.5 + 3 = 74.5 cm finished, plus 1.5 + 1.5 cm seam allowances = 77.5 cm.

quiz.q: Elastic keeps twisting inside a child's skirt casing. What should she do?
options: Use thinner elastic in a much wider casing
Stitch in the ditch through casing and elastic at the side seams
quiz.explain: Stitching through the elastic at the side seams holds it in place so it cannot roll or twist.

quiz.q: Which waist finish best suits a fitted lace occasion dress with no visible band?
quiz.explain: A faced waist gives a clean, bandless finish for fitted dressy styles; understitching keeps the facing inside.

modules.title: Zips, Buttons and Closures That Work Every Time
modules.overview: A closure is a moving part: it is opened and closed hundreds of times. This module covers the invisible zip, lapped, centred, exposed and fly zips, and buttons, buttonholes, hooks and loops, with the measurements and checks that make them both neat and durable.

lessons.title: Installing an invisible zip that truly disappears
objectives: Choose the right invisible zip length for an opening
Prepare the zip coil and seam before sewing
Install an invisible zip with an invisible zip foot so the seam meets cleanly
Close the seam below the zip without a bubble or pucker

blocks.text: An **invisible zip** (also called a concealed zip) has its coil on the back of the tape. Once sewn, the garment looks like a normal seam; only the small pull tab shows at the top. It is the standard closure for fitted dresses, skirts and occasion wear, including lace and aso-ebi styles. It is not difficult, but it rewards careful preparation and punishes rushing.

blocks.name: dress
blocks.caption: Fitted dresses and skirts rely on an invisible zip in the centre back or side seam.

blocks.text: Choosing the zip

items: Buy an invisible zip at least **2 to 3 cm longer** than the opening. The slider and stopper take up space at the bottom, and you cannot sew right to the end of the coil.
Match the zip colour to the fabric. On lace, choose the colour of the base fabric or lining, not the lace motif.
Use a lightweight zip for chiffon, crepe and cotton; a heavier one only for thick fabrics that will strain the closure.
Get an **invisible zip foot** (it has two grooves under it) for your machine. A regular zip foot works only with extra care and gives a less hidden result.

blocks.text: Preparing

items: Do **not** sew the seam below the zip yet. The zip goes in first.
Finish the seam allowance edges (overlock or zigzag) before inserting the zip.

Fuse a strip of light interfacing, about 2 cm wide, to the wrong side of each seam allowance where the zip will go. This stops the seam stretching and waving, especially on knits, crepe and bias-cut fabric.
Mark the seam line with chalk and mark the end point of the opening on both sides.

Open the zip and press the coil away from the tape from the wrong side, using a low iron (synthetic setting) and no steam. This uncurls the coil so the needle can sew right beside it. Do not let the iron touch the coil directly.

blocks.text: Sewing the zip

items: With the zip open, place it face down on the right side of the left garment piece, with the coil exactly on the seam line and the top stop just below the waist or neck seam line.
Put the coil in the right-hand groove of the invisible zip foot. Sew from the top down until the foot touches the slider. Backstitch.
Close the zip and check it lies flat. Mark on the second tape where the waist seam and any cross seams must match.
Open the zip. Pin the second tape to the right garment piece, face down, coil on the seam line, matching your marks.
Sew with the coil in the left-hand groove, from top to bottom again. Sewing both sides in the same direction prevents twisting.
Close the zip and check both sides from the right side before you continue.

blocks.title: Invisible zip order of work
items: Finish and stabilise allowances
Press coil flat
Sew first side top down
Mark and sew second side
Close seam below zip
blocks.caption: Doing these steps in this order is what makes the zip vanish into the seam.

blocks.text: Closing the seam below the zip

Switch to a regular zip foot. Close the zip. Pull the zip tape ends out of the way towards the seam allowance. Start sewing the seam about 1 cm above the bottom of the zip stitching and about 2 mm to the left of it, so the two lines of stitching overlap slightly without crossing onto the coil. Sew down the rest of the seam. Then stitch the bottom ends of the zip tape to the seam allowances only, so the zip cannot flap.

blocks.title: Worked example: matching the waist seam across a zip
blocks.context: For example, Tolu in Ilorin is making a fitted dress with a waist seam. The 56 cm centre back opening runs from the neckline to below the waist.
steps: She buys a 60 cm invisible zip, 4 cm longer than the opening.
After sewing the first side, she closes the zip and marks the waist seam and the neckline position on the second tape with chalk.
When pinning the second side, she lines up these marks exactly with the waist seam and neckline on the right back piece.
She checks from the right side: the waist seams meet within 1 mm, so she continues.
blocks.result: The waist seam lines up straight across the back, the zip is hidden, and only the pull tab shows at the neckline.

blocks.title: Common faults
blocks.text: A bubble at the bottom of the zip means the seam below started too far away from the zip stitching. Visible zip tape means the coil was not pressed flat or the foot rode away from the coil. Waving or rippling means the seam allowance was not stabilised. Fix the cause before you resew.
Lace and lined garments

On lace over a lining, treat the lace and its base fabric as one layer: tack them together along the seam allowance before inserting the zip, so the lace cannot shift. Where the lace has a scalloped or motif edge near the zip, make sure the pattern lines up on both sides at the top, because a mismatch at the neckline is very visible. If the dress has a separate lining, the lining is folded back and slip-stitched to the zip tape later, which you will learn in Module 4.

takeaways: Buy the invisible zip 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening
Stabilise the seam allowances and press the coil flat first
Sew both sides from top to bottom and match cross seams
Overlap the seam stitching slightly at the bottom to avoid a bubble

activity.title: Invisible zip sample
steps: Cut two fabric pieces 15 cm by 30 cm and draw a cross line 10 cm from the top on both as a pretend waist seam.
Stabilise the allowances and press the coil of a 25 cm or longer invisible zip.
Insert the zip, matching the cross lines, and close the seam below.
Photograph the right side close up and measure how far the cross lines miss each other.
activity.evidence: Close-up photo of the zip sample and the cross line difference in millimetres

lessons.title: Lapped, centred, exposed and fly-front zips
objectives: Choose between lapped, centred, exposed and fly zips for a style
Sew a lapped zip with an even topstitching line
Explain the parts of a trouser fly front
Keep topstitching straight and an even distance from the seam

blocks.text: Not every garment needs an invisible zip. Regular **coil or metal zips**, with teeth on the front of the tape, are stronger and easier to repair. They are used on trousers, jeans, casual skirts, children's wear, bags and jackets. How you set the zip into the seam decides how it looks: hidden under a lap, centred between two folds, deliberately on show, or behind a fly.

blocks.name: jeans
blocks.caption: Trousers and jeans use a fly-front zip, a lapped zip with an extra shield behind it.

head: Zip setting
How it looks
Good for
Key point
rows: Lapped
One fold covers the teeth; one row of topstitching shows
Skirt side seams, dress side or back seams
The lap must fully cover the teeth
Centred
Two folds meet over the centre of the teeth; two rows of topstitching
Centre back of dresses and skirts
Both stitching lines the same distance from the seam
Exposed
Teeth fully visible as a design feature
Modern styles, jackets, bags
Neat box at the bottom and straight edges
Fly front
A lap with a curved row of stitching on the front
Trousers, jeans, shorts
A fly shield behind protects skin and teeth

blocks.text: Sewing a lapped zip

items: Sew the seam below the opening with normal stitches, then machine-tack (long stitches) the opening closed along the seam line. Press the seam open.
On the **underlap** side, fold the seam allowance so the fold sits about 3 mm out from the seam line. Press.
Place this fold right next to the zip teeth and sew it to the tape with a zip foot, from bottom to top.
Lay the garment right side up. The lap side now covers the teeth because of the original seam line.
Topstitch the lap through all layers, about 1 to 1.5 cm from the fold, across the bottom and up the side. Use a strip of masking tape as a guide.
Remove the tacking stitches. The fold now hides the zip completely.

blocks.text: Centred and exposed zips in brief

For a **centred zip**, tack the opening closed, press it open, and place the zip face down centred on the seam on the wrong side. Hold it with tape or tacking, then topstitch from the right side at the same distance, for example 7 mm, each side and across the bottom. Remove the tacking. For an **exposed zip**, cut a narrow window or fold the seam allowances back so the teeth show, place the zip under the folds and edge-stitch close to each fold. A small rectangle of interfacing at the bottom of the window prevents tearing.
Fly front: the parts

items: **Fly extension**: a strip cut in one with the front trouser piece, or added, that becomes the lap.
**Fly facing**: the inside layer behind the lap, often interfaced.
**Fly shield**: a separate folded strip on the other side, behind the zip, that protects the body from the teeth and supports the button.
**J-stitch**: the curved line of topstitching on the front that holds the lap, usually about 3 to 4 cm from the centre front.

blocks.text: In practice, the order is: sew the zip to the fly facing on one side, attach the other zip tape to the folded fly shield and the opposite front, then sew the J-stitch from the right side using a paper or card template so the curve is smooth. Finish with a bar tack at the bottom of the curve, where the fly takes the most strain when the wearer sits down.

blocks.title: Lapped zip or invisible zip?
items: Lapped zip
Invisible zip
left: Strong; regular zip is easy to repair
Good for casual and heavier fabrics
right: Best for fitted dresses and occasion wear
Needs special foot and careful matching
blocks.caption: Pick the setting that matches the fabric, the style and how hard the closure will work.

blocks.title: Worked example: planning even topstitching
blocks.context: For example, Ruth in Kaduna is making a centre back centred zip in a navy cotton skirt. Her zip teeth and tape together are 2.5 cm wide.
steps: She chooses a topstitching distance of 7 mm on each side of the seam, so the two rows are 14 mm apart and both rows fall on the zip tape, clear of the teeth.
She sticks a 7 mm wide strip of masking tape along each side of the seam on the right side as a guide.
At the bottom she stitches straight across, 1 cm below the zip stop, so the needle never hits the metal stop.
She uses a stitch length of 3 mm in matching thread, because longer stitches look neater as topstitching.
blocks.result: Both rows of topstitching are straight and the same 7 mm from the seam, and the needle never strikes the zip stop.

blocks.title: Needles and metal zips
blocks.text: Never sew over the metal teeth or the stopper of a metal zip. The needle can break and fly up. Walk the machine by hand near the stop, wear glasses if you have them, and keep your face back from the needle area.

Whichever setting you use, test the zip several times before the garment leaves your table: it should run smoothly from top to bottom, the pull tab should lie flat, and no fabric should get caught in the teeth.

takeaways: Regular zips are stronger and easier to repair than invisible zips
A lapped zip hides the teeth under one fold and one row of topstitching
Keep topstitching the same distance from the seam with a tape guide
Never sew over metal teeth or the zip stop

steps: Cut two pieces of cotton 15 cm by 30 cm and sew a 10 cm seam at one end.
Insert a 20 cm regular zip as a lapped zip using a masking tape guide.
Measure the topstitching distance from the fold at three points.
Photograph the right side and record the three measurements.
