lessons.title: Buttons, buttonholes, hooks and loops that last
objectives: Calculate buttonhole length and button spacing
Sew a machine buttonhole and open it safely
Sew a button with a thread shank so the closure lies flat
Attach hooks and eyes, hooks and bars, snaps and button loops correctly

blocks.text: Buttons and buttonholes are a small part of the garment but a large part of how clients judge your work. A buttonhole with frayed edges, or a button that falls off after the first wash, is the kind of fault people tell their friends about. The good news is that strong, neat closures come from a few simple rules followed every time.

blocks.name: black-square-button
blocks.caption: Every button needs a correctly sized buttonhole and a thread shank to sit well.

blocks.text: Sizing and spacing

items: **Buttonhole length = button diameter + button thickness.** For a domed or very thick button, add a little more, then test.
Interface the area under buttonholes, usually the front facing or placket, so the hole does not stretch.
Vertical buttonholes are used on narrow plackets; horizontal ones on waistbands, cuffs and wider fronts because they resist strain better.
A horizontal buttonhole starts about 3 mm **beyond** the centre front line towards the edge, so the button sits exactly on centre front when closed.
Place a button at the point of most strain, such as the bust line on a fitted blouse, and space the others evenly from there.

blocks.title: Worked example: spacing blouse buttons
blocks.context: For example, Joy in Calabar is making a fitted blouse. The first button sits 1.5 cm below the neckline, and the last button must sit 42 cm below the first. She wants 7 buttons. The buttons are 15 mm across and 3 mm thick.
steps: Seven buttons means six spaces between them.
Spacing: 42 cm divided by 6 is 7 cm between button centres.
She checks the bust line: it falls 21 cm below the first button, which is exactly where button 4 lands (3 spaces times 7 cm), so there is no gaping.
Buttonhole length: 15 mm plus 3 mm equals 18 mm. She sews a test buttonhole on scrap with the interfacing and checks the button passes through easily.
blocks.result: Seven buttons spaced 7 cm apart, one sitting on the bust line, with 18 mm buttonholes that open smoothly.

blocks.text: Machine buttonhole and opening it safely

items: Mark each buttonhole with chalk or a fabric pen: a line for the length and a short cross line at each end.
Use the buttonhole foot and the setting in your manual. Many machines have a one-step foot where you put the button in the back of the foot to set the length.
Always sew a test on a scrap with the same layers and interfacing.
To open, put a pin across each end just inside the bar tack. Cut from the middle towards each end with a seam ripper or small sharp scissors. The pins stop you cutting through the bar.
Dab a tiny amount of fray stopper on the cut edges if the fabric frays easily, testing it on scrap first.

blocks.text: Sewing on a button with a shank

A flat sew-through button needs space between it and the fabric for the buttonhole layer to sit under it. This space is the **thread shank**. Without a shank, the button pulls the fabric, the closure puckers and the threads wear through quickly.

items: Use double thread, or buttonhole thread for coats and heavy fabrics. Knot and take a small stitch on the right side where the button goes.
Lay a matchstick or toothpick on top of the button between the holes.
Sew through the holes and over the stick 5 or 6 times, in two parallel bars or a cross.
Remove the stick, pull the button up and wrap the thread round the stitches under the button 4 or 5 times to form the shank.
Take the needle to the wrong side and finish with several small stitches through the thread on the back.

blocks.title: Button order of work
items: Interface the placket
Mark and test buttonholes
Sew and open buttonholes
Mark buttons through holes
Sew buttons with shanks
blocks.caption: Buttonholes come first; then mark each button through its hole so they line up exactly.

blocks.text: Hooks, eyes, bars, snaps and loops

head: Closure
Where it is used
How to sew it well
rows: Hook and eye
Top of a zip at the neck, edge-to-edge openings
Set the hook 2 to 3 mm in from the edge; sew round each loop and across the neck of the hook so it cannot tilt
Hook and bar
Waistbands of skirts and trousers
Sew through every hole with several stitches; it takes strain, so stitch through the interfacing
Snap fastener
Light closures, overlaps that need no strain
Put the ball half on the overlap, socket on the underlap; sew through each hole 4 or 5 times
Button loop
Bridal and occasion backs, kaftan necklines
Make loops from a narrow bias tube or thread chain, all the same size, sewn into the seam

blocks.title: Wash test for orders
blocks.text: For school uniforms or group orders, wash one sample garment once before delivering the batch. Check that buttons are still tight and buttonholes have not frayed. It is far cheaper to adjust your method than to resew buttons on fifty shirts.

takeaways: Buttonhole length equals button diameter plus thickness, then test
Interface every buttonhole area and test on scrap
Put pins across buttonhole ends before cutting them open
Every sew-through button needs a thread shank

activity.title: Closure practice card
steps: Interface a 20 cm by 10 cm strip of cotton, fold it in half and press.
Sew three buttonholes sized for one of your buttons and open them safely.
Sew three buttons with thread shanks on a matching strip.
Add one hook and bar and one snap, then button the card closed and photograph it.
activity.evidence: Photo of the finished closure practice card, front and back

quiz.q: The zip opening on a dress is 50 cm. What invisible zip length should she buy?
quiz.explain: An invisible zip should be at least 2 to 3 cm longer than the opening, because you cannot sew to the very end of the coil.

quiz.q: There is a small bubble just below an invisible zip. What caused it?
options: The coil was pressed too flat
The seam below started too far from the end of the zip stitching
quiz.explain: The seam below must start slightly above and just to the side of the zip stitching so the two lines meet without a gap.

quiz.q: A button is 20 mm across and 4 mm thick. What is the starting buttonhole length?
quiz.explain: Button diameter plus thickness: 20 + 4 = 24 mm. Then test on scrap.

quiz.q: Buttons on a shirt pucker the front and keep falling off. What was most likely missing?
quiz.explain: Without a thread shank the button pulls the fabric tight and the threads wear through quickly.

quiz.q: Eight buttons must fit between 1.5 cm below the neck and 50.5 cm below the neck. What is the spacing?
quiz.explain: The span is 50.5 - 1.5 = 49 cm. Eight buttons make seven spaces, and 49 divided by 7 is 7 cm.

quiz.q: Which closure is usually best for the waistband of fitted trousers?
quiz.explain: A hook and bar takes strain well and lies flat, which is why it is standard on trouser and skirt waistbands.

quiz.q: Why place a pin across each end of a buttonhole before cutting it open?
options: To stop the blade cutting through the bar tack
quiz.explain: The pin acts as a stop, so the cut cannot slice the bar tack at the end of the buttonhole.

modules.title: Linings, Piping, Binding and Decorative Details
modules.overview: Linings make a garment comfortable and hang well; piping, binding and embellishment make it distinctive. This module teaches how to choose and fit a lining with the right ease, cut and apply bias for piping and binding, and add appliqué, beading, lace and embroidery that stay secure and are priced for the time they take.

lessons.title: Lining a skirt, dress or jacket with the right fabric and ease
objectives: Choose a lining fabric for the garment, climate and budget
Cut and sew a lining with enough ease so it never pulls the outer fabric
Finish a lining neatly at the zip and the hem
Explain the jump pleat in a jacket lining and why it is needed

blocks.text: A **lining** is a separate inner layer that covers the seams and inside of a garment. It helps the garment slide on, stops scratchy fabrics such as lace, wool blends and sequins touching the skin, makes sheer fabrics opaque, and helps the outer fabric hang without clinging. A badly fitted lining does the opposite: it pulls the outer fabric, peeps out at the hem, or makes the garment hot and uncomfortable.

blocks.name: kimono
blocks.caption: Flowing and structured garments both depend on a lining that is cut and fitted with care.

blocks.text: Choosing lining fabric

head: Lining
Feel and behaviour
Good for
Watch out for
rows: Polyester lining
Smooth, slippery, affordable, washable
Everyday skirts, dresses and jackets
Can feel hot in Nigerian heat; does not breathe well
Viscose or cupro (often sold as Bemberg)
Breathable, smooth, drapes like silk
Quality dresses and jackets, boutique work
Costs more; can shrink, so pre-wash or steam
Cotton lawn or voile
Light, cool, not slippery
Children's wear, casual dresses, hot climates
Clings to tights; less smooth to slide on
Satin or taffeta lining
Shiny, firm, luxurious look
Bridal and evening wear, structured skirts
Can be warm and noisy; heat-sensitive when pressing
Stretch lining or power mesh
Stretches with the body
Bodycon and stretch dresses
Must stretch as much as the outer fabric

blocks.title: Climate matters
blocks.text: In hot, humid weather, many clients find full polyester linings sticky. For day dresses, consider cotton voile or a viscose lining, or line only the parts that need it, such as the bodice of a lace dress.
Ease: why linings must not be tight

Linings are less stretchy than most outer fabrics, and they sit inside, so they need a little extra room. A common approach is to cut the lining from the same pattern pieces, but to sew the **vertical lining seams slightly smaller**, for example 3 to 5 mm inside the garment seam line at each seam, and to turn darts into soft unpressed tucks. This adds width across the body so the lining never strains.
Lining a straight skirt step by step

items: Cut lining pieces from the skirt pattern. Mark the lining hem to finish about 2 to 2.5 cm above the finished skirt hem.
Sew the lining side seams and centre back seam, leaving the zip opening plus about 1 cm unsewn. Leave the vent area open if the skirt has a vent.
Place the lining inside the skirt, wrong sides together. Match side seams and centre back, and tack the lining to the skirt along the waist seam allowance.
Attach the waistband or facing through both layers as one.
At the zip, fold under the lining seam allowance so the fold sits 3 to 5 mm away from the zip coil, and slip-stitch it to the zip tape. The slider must not catch the lining.
Hem the skirt and the lining separately. Join them at each side seam with a **French tack**: a thread chain about 2 to 3 cm long that lets the lining move but keeps it in place.

blocks.title: Layers in a lined skirt
items: Outer fashion fabric
Seams and allowances
Lining with extra ease
French tacks at hem
blocks.caption: The lining covers the seams and moves freely, held loosely at the hem by French tacks.

blocks.text: Jackets: the jump pleat

In a jacket, the lining is attached at the hem and the sleeve hems, so it needs spare length for movement. Two folds of spare fabric give this: a **centre back pleat**, often about 2 to 3 cm deep, tacked at the neck and waist, and a **jump pleat** at the hem, where the lining is sewn to the jacket hem allowance and then a fold of about 1 to 1.5 cm is allowed to hang down over the stitching. When the wearer reaches forward, these pleats open instead of the lining pulling on the jacket.

blocks.title: Worked example: fixing a lining that pulls
blocks.context: For example, Patience in Abeokuta finished a lined lace dress, but the outer lace wrinkles across the hips when the client sits. The lining was sewn on exactly the same seam lines as the dress.
steps: She unpicks the lining from the waist seam at the side seams only, not the whole waist.
She resews each lining side seam 4 mm further into the seam allowance from the hip down, so the front piece and the back piece each gain 4 mm at that seam: 8 mm per side seam.
Total extra width: two side seams times 8 mm is 16 mm, about 1.6 cm round the hips.
She re-tacks the lining at the waist and checks again with the client seated.
blocks.result: With about 1.6 cm extra width in the lining, the lace lies smoothly over the hips when the client sits.

blocks.title: Pre-shrink when in doubt
blocks.text: If a garment will be washed at home, wash or steam the lining and the outer fabric before cutting, especially viscose and cotton. If they shrink by different amounts later, the lining will either hang below the hem or pull the outer fabric up.

takeaways: Choose lining by comfort, climate, garment use and budget
Give linings extra ease: sew vertical seams slightly smaller
Hem the lining separately, about 2 to 2.5 cm above the garment hem
Jacket linings need a centre back pleat and a jump pleat

activity.title: Lining choice and ease plan
steps: Choose two garments you might make this month and note their outer fabric.
For each, choose a lining from the table and write why.
Write the lining hem position and the seam allowance change you would use.
Make a 3 cm French tack on scrap fabric and photograph it.
activity.evidence: Lining plan for two garments and a photo of your French tack

lessons.title: Cutting bias strips and applying piping and binding
objectives: Find the true bias and cut bias strips accurately
Calculate bias strip width for piping and binding
Make and insert piping into a seam so it is even all round
Bind a neckline or armhole with a flat, smooth finish

blocks.text: **Piping** is a narrow fabric-covered cord sewn into a seam so it shows as a thin raised line. **Binding** is a strip of fabric that wraps around a raw edge to finish it. Both are made from **bias strips**: fabric cut at 45 degrees to the threads. Cut this way, fabric stretches and bends smoothly around curves such as necklines, armholes and rounded hems, which straight-grain strips cannot do.

blocks.name: black-scissors
blocks.caption: Accurate bias strips start with accurate cutting at 45 degrees.

blocks.text: Finding the bias and cutting strips

items: Straighten one cut edge of the fabric along a thread, and find the selvedge (the woven edge).
Fold the straight edge down so it lies along the selvedge. The diagonal fold is the **true bias**.
Press the fold lightly, open it and draw parallel lines at your strip width with a ruler and chalk.
Cut the strips, then join them on the straight grain: place two strip ends right sides together at a right angle, sew diagonally, trim to 6 mm and press open.

blocks.text: How wide to cut

For **piping**, the strip must wrap the cord and leave two seam allowances. Width = cord circumference + two seam allowances. Circumference is about 3.14 times the cord diameter. For **double-fold binding** that finishes 1 cm wide, you need four times the finished width, so about 4 cm. For **French (double-layer) binding**, which is folded in half first and is stronger on lightweight fabric, cut about six times the finished width.

blocks.title: Worked example: piping a cushion and a kaftan neckline
blocks.context: For example, Rahila in Abuja is adding piping in a contrast colour to a kaftan neckline that measures 64 cm. She uses 4 mm piping cord and a 1.5 cm seam allowance.
steps: Cord circumference: 4 mm times 3.14 is about 12.6 mm, round up to 1.3 cm.
Strip width: 1.3 cm plus 1.5 cm plus 1.5 cm equals 4.3 cm; she cuts 4.5 cm for an easy margin.
Strip length: 64 cm neckline plus about 6 cm for joining and overlapping is 70 cm.
From a 50 cm square, the diagonal is 50 times 1.414, about 70.7 cm, so one strip along the diagonal is just enough. She cuts two to be safe.
blocks.result: She cuts 4.5 cm wide bias strips at least 70 cm long, giving even piping all round the neckline with a neat join at the back.

blocks.text: Making and inserting piping

items: Wrap the bias strip around the cord, wrong sides together, raw edges level.
Sew close to the cord with a zip foot or piping foot, but not tight against it.
Trim the piping seam allowance to match the garment seam allowance.
Pin the piping to the right side of one garment piece, raw edges together, and sew just inside the first line of stitching.
Clip the piping allowance on curves so it lies flat.
Place the second piece on top and sew again, this time slightly closer to the cord, so the first stitching is hidden.

blocks.title: Piping or binding?
items: Piping
Binding
left: Needs cord and a zip foot
blocks.caption: Use piping to outline a seam, and binding to finish an edge.

blocks.text: Binding a neckline

Sew the binding to the right side of the neckline at the finished width, for example 1 cm from the edge for a 1 cm binding. Stretch the binding very slightly around inward curves such as the front neck, and ease it slightly around outward curves. Fold the binding over the edge to the inside, fold under the raw edge, and stitch in the ditch from the right side or slip-stitch by hand. Press with steam, shaping the curve as you press.

blocks.title: Contrast details sell
blocks.text: A contrast binding or piping on plain or ankara garments is a small detail that clients often notice and recognise as your style. Record the time it takes, for example 30 to 40 minutes for a neckline and sleeve hems, and include that time in your price.
Troubleshooting piping and binding

head: Problem
Likely cause
Fix
rows: Piping looks thick in some places and thin in others
Seam allowance not kept even, or final seam wandered
Trim piping allowance to exactly match the garment allowance and sew with the zip foot pressed against the cord
Binding twists or ripples on a curve
Strip cut off the true bias, or stretched unevenly
Recut on the true bias and shape the strip with steam before sewing
Lumps where strips are joined
Joins sewn straight across instead of diagonally
Join on the straight grain with a diagonal seam and press it open
Binding edge does not catch underneath
Folded edge not long enough to pass the first seam
Press binding so the inside fold reaches 1 to 2 mm past the seam before stitching in the ditch

blocks.text: Prints need extra thought. On ankara, a small-scale print or a plain colour usually makes better binding than a large motif, because large motifs get cut into confusing fragments in a 1 cm strip. Stripes cut on the bias turn into diagonals, which can make a striking candy-stripe trim.

takeaways: Bias strips are cut at 45 degrees so they bend round curves
Piping width = cord circumference + two seam allowances
Double-fold binding needs about four times the finished width
Clip piping on curves and sew the final seam closer to the cord

activity.title: Bias, piping and binding samples
steps: Find the true bias on a 50 cm square and cut four strips 4 cm wide.
Join two strips with a diagonal seam and press it open.
Make 30 cm of piping and insert it into a curved seam sample.
Bind one curved edge with 1 cm double-fold binding and photograph both samples.
activity.evidence: Photos of the piping and binding samples, with your strip width calculation

lessons.title: Appliqué, beading, lace and embroidery that stay secure
objectives: Apply fused appliqué with a satin stitch edge that does not fray
Secure beads and sequins so they do not fall off in wear
Apply lace motifs and overlays without distorting the pattern
Price decorative work from the time and materials it takes

blocks.text: Decorative details turn a plain garment into an occasion piece. Aso-ebi lace, beaded bodices, embroidered agbada necklines and ankara appliqué are part of Nigerian fashion life. Done well, they justify a higher price. Done badly, with loose threads, puckering or beads falling on the dance floor, they damage your reputation. The difference is in **stabilising, securing and checking**.

blocks.name: gem-stone
blocks.caption: Beads and stones must be secured so they stay on through dancing, sitting and cleaning.

blocks.text: Appliqué

items: Fuse a double-sided fusible web to the back of the appliqué fabric, following the maker's instructions. Draw your shape on the paper backing and cut it out.
Peel the paper, position the shape on the garment and press to fuse it.
Place a tear-away or iron-on stabiliser behind the garment under the motif so the stitching does not pucker.
Sew round the edge with a close zigzag (satin stitch), about 2 to 3 mm wide with a very short stitch length, so the raw edge is fully covered.
On curves, stop with the needle down on the outside of the curve, lift the foot, turn slightly and continue. Remove the stabiliser carefully.

blocks.text: Beads and sequins

items: Use a fine beading needle and a strong thread such as polyester or a dedicated beading thread. Run it through beeswax or thread conditioner to stop tangles.
Hoop the fabric or work over a firm stabiliser so the base fabric does not pucker.
**Backstitch and knot regularly**: secure the thread every 3 or 4 beads with a tiny backstitch, so if one thread breaks only a few beads come off, not a whole line.
Do not carry thread long distances on the back; tie off and start again. Long floats catch on jewellery and snap.
Sew sequins with a small seed bead on top, or overlap them so each stitch is hidden by the next sequin.

blocks.text: Lace motifs and overlays

Lace overlays look most expensive when the pattern flows across seams and the edges follow the motifs. Lay the lace on the garment piece and move it until the main motifs sit symmetrically on centre front, the bust and the hem. Tack it to the base fabric. Where lace meets lace at a seam, you can overlap motifs and cut round them, then join them by hand or with a narrow zigzag so the seam disappears into the pattern. Trim the base fabric away behind if you want a sheer effect.
Embroidery

Whether by hand or machine, embroidery needs the fabric held firmly and supported. Hoop the fabric drum-tight but not stretched out of shape, with a stabiliser behind it suited to the fabric (tear-away for stable wovens, cut-away for knits). Test the design and thread tension on scrap. After stitching, remove hoop marks by steaming from the back on a towel so the stitches are not flattened.

blocks.title: Embellishment quality check
items: No raw or loose edges
No puckering of base fabric
Thread secured every few beads
Design centred and symmetrical
No long floats on back
blocks.caption: Check every embellished panel against these five points before attaching it to the garment.

blocks.title: Worked example: pricing a beaded neckline
blocks.context: For example, Fatima in Lagos is quoting for a hand-beaded neckline on an aso-ebi lace blouse. She times a 5 cm test section at 20 minutes. The neckline to bead is 60 cm long. She values her time at 1,500 naira an hour (her own figure, approximate) and materials at about 4,000 naira.
steps: Sections: 60 cm divided by 5 cm is 12 sections.
Time: 12 sections times 20 minutes is 240 minutes, which is 4 hours.
Labour: 4 hours times 1,500 naira is 6,000 naira.
Add materials: 6,000 plus about 4,000 is about 10,000 naira for the beading.
She adds this to her price for the blouse and explains the beading cost separately to the client.
blocks.result: The beading adds about 10,000 naira (approximate) to the price, based on measured time and real materials, not guesswork.

blocks.title: Care for embellished garments
blocks.text: Many beads, sequins and metallic threads cannot take a hot iron or machine washing. Press embellished areas only from the back on a thick towel with a press cloth, and tell the client how the garment should be cleaned. Put this on the care card you give at handover.
Plan the order of work

Embellish garment pieces **flat, before** they are sewn together wherever possible: it is easier to hoop, easier to keep symmetrical, and you can check both sides. Leave about 2 cm clear of beads at each seam allowance so the machine foot can pass, then fill those gaps by hand after the seams are sewn. Agree the design with the client first using a sketch or a photo of a sample panel, and keep that agreement in your order notes. A client who has approved a sample panel is far less likely to dispute the finished piece.

takeaways: Stabilise fabric behind appliqué, beading and embroidery
Secure beads every 3 or 4 with a backstitch and avoid long floats
Place lace motifs symmetrically and let them flow across seams
Price embellishment from timed samples plus materials

activity.title: Embellishment sample and price
steps: Make a 10 cm by 10 cm appliqué sample with a satin stitch edge.
Bead a 5 cm line, securing every 3 or 4 beads, and time yourself.
Use your time to estimate the hours for a 60 cm neckline.
Write a price for that neckline using your own hourly rate and material costs.
activity.evidence: Photos of both samples, front and back, plus your timing and price calculation

quiz.q: A lining is pulling the lace dress across the hips. What is the best fix?
options: Let out the lining side seams a few millimetres so the lining has more ease
Sew the lining to the lace all over
quiz.explain: Linings need slightly more width than the outer garment. Letting out the vertical seams adds ease so the outer fabric lies smoothly.

quiz.q: Where should a skirt lining hem finish?
options: About 2 to 2.5 cm above the skirt hem
At the knee whatever the skirt length
quiz.explain: Finishing the lining about 2 to 2.5 cm above the hem keeps it hidden when the client walks and sits.

quiz.q: Piping cord is 3 mm in diameter and the seam allowance is 1 cm. About what width should the bias strip be?
quiz.explain: Circumference is about 3 x 3.14 = 9.4 mm, about 1 cm. Add two 1 cm allowances: about 3 cm.

quiz.q: Why are piping and binding strips cut on the bias?
options: Bias-cut fabric bends smoothly around curves
Bias strips do not need pressing
quiz.explain: Fabric cut at 45 degrees to the threads stretches and shapes around curves such as necklines and armholes.

quiz.q: A client says beads keep falling off a whole line at a time. What should the maker change?
options: Backstitch to secure the thread every 3 or 4 beads
Carry the thread further between beads
quiz.explain: Securing every few beads means a broken thread only loses a few beads, not a whole row.

quiz.q: A 5 cm beaded test takes 15 minutes. How long would an 80 cm neckline take?
quiz.explain: 80 / 5 = 16 sections. 16 x 15 minutes = 240 minutes = 4 hours.

quiz.q: What does the jump pleat in a jacket lining do?
options: Hides the hem stitches and gives spare length for movement
quiz.explain: The jump pleat hangs over the hem stitching and opens when the wearer moves, so the lining does not pull on the jacket.

modules.title: Quality Control: Inspecting, Correcting and Handing Over
modules.overview: Quality control is a system, not a feeling. In this module you build a written inspection routine with measurement tolerances, classify faults by how serious they are, trace each fault to its cause and fix it, and finish with a final press, care card and handover that protect your reputation.

lessons.title: A written inspection routine: the 12-point check, spec sheet and tolerances
objectives: Inspect a garment in a fixed order using a 12-point checklist
Measure a finished garment against a spec sheet with tolerances
Classify faults as critical, major or minor
Decide pass, fix or reject for a single garment and for a batch

blocks.text: Every maker checks her work, but most check it **from memory**, quickly, at the end of a long day. That is when faults slip through. Professional workrooms and garment factories use a written routine: the same points, in the same order, recorded on paper or a phone, for every garment. The written record also protects you if a client later complains.

blocks.name: inspection
blocks.alt: A person inspecting an item closely
blocks.caption: Inspection works best as a fixed routine, written down, done in good light.

blocks.text: Set up for inspection

items: Good light: daylight near a window, or a bright white bulb. Dark fabrics hide faults under yellow light.
A clean table, a hanger or dress form, a tape measure, a small pair of thread snips and a pen.
The order card with the client's measurements and the agreed style, fabric and finish.
Your checklist sheet or a simple form on your phone, one per garment.

blocks.text: The 12-point check, in order
Work **outside to inside, top to bottom**, so you never skip an area. First on the hanger or form, then flat on the table, then inside out.

head: No.
Point
What passes
rows: Overall look on hanger
Hangs straight, no twisting, both sides symmetrical
Collar or neckline
Lies flat, both sides match, no under collar or facing showing
Shoulders and sleeves
Sleeve caps smooth, no puckers; cuffs match
Closures
Zip runs smoothly; buttons secure with shanks; buttonholes clean
Pattern matching
Prints, stripes and checks match at centre front, centre back and side seams
Seams
Straight, even width, no skipped stitches, no puckering
Topstitching
Same distance from the edge all along, consistent stitch length
Hem
Level when hung, invisible or neat as agreed, no ripples
Embellishment
All beads and motifs secure, no loose edges
Inside finish
Seam edges finished, lining hangs freely, no raw edges
Threads and marks
All thread ends trimmed; no chalk, pen or glue marks
Measurements
Key measurements within tolerance on the spec sheet

blocks.text: Spec sheet and tolerances

A **spec sheet** lists the key finished measurements of the garment: bust, waist, hip, length, sleeve length and so on. A **tolerance** is how far a measurement may differ and still pass, for example plus or minus 0.5 cm on a cuff or plus or minus 1 cm on a skirt length. You set your own tolerances, tighter for fitted, bespoke garments and a little wider for loose styles. Measure the garment flat and compare.

blocks.title: Worked example: checking a dress against its spec
blocks.context: For example, Amaka in Enugu has finished a fitted dress. Her spec sheet says finished bust 96 cm, waist 80 cm, hip 104 cm and length 110 cm, with a tolerance of plus or minus 1 cm for each.
steps: She measures flat across the bust, 48.5 cm, and doubles it: 97 cm. That is 1 cm over, inside tolerance: pass.
Waist: 40.5 cm doubled is 81 cm, 1 cm over: pass.
Hip: 51.8 cm doubled is 103.6 cm, 0.4 cm under: pass.
Length from the shoulder at the neck point: 108.5 cm. That is 1.5 cm short, outside tolerance: fail.
She checks the hem allowance: 3 cm was turned up. She lets the hem down by 1.5 cm, leaving a 1.5 cm allowance, and rehems with a narrow finish.
blocks.result: Bust, waist and hip pass; the length failed by 0.5 cm beyond tolerance and was corrected before handover.

blocks.text: How serious is each fault?

Garment factories commonly sort faults into three levels. A **critical** fault makes the garment unsafe, for example a broken needle left inside, a sharp metal edge, or a loose small button on a baby's garment that could be swallowed. A **major** fault would make the client unhappy or the garment fail: a seam opening, a zip that sticks, a hem visibly uneven. A **minor** fault is a small workmanship flaw that does not affect use, such as one untrimmed thread inside. Critical faults are never accepted. Major faults must be fixed before handover. Minor faults are fixed whenever possible and recorded.

blocks.title: Fault levels and actions
items: Critical: never accept
Major: fix before handover
Minor: fix and record
blocks.caption: The more serious the fault, the stronger the action: critical faults stop the garment completely.

blocks.title: Needles and pins
blocks.text: Count pins and hand needles before and after each job, use a magnet or pin cushion, and run your hand and a magnet over children's garments before handover. A broken machine needle tip must be found before the garment leaves the workroom.
Batch orders

For aso-ebi and uniform orders of a few dozen pieces, check **every** garment against the checklist and measure every piece at a few key points. Large factories inspect random samples using published sampling tables such as ANSI/ASQ Z1.4 and ISO 2859-1, with an agreed Acceptable Quality Limit (AQL); that is useful to know if you ever supply a retailer, but for a small workroom, 100 percent inspection is realistic and safer.

takeaways: Inspect in a fixed order: outside to inside, top to bottom
Compare measurements with a spec sheet and set tolerances
Critical faults are never accepted; major faults are fixed before handover
Small batches: inspect every piece

activity.title: Inspect a finished garment
steps: Copy the 12-point checklist into a notebook or phone note.
Write a spec sheet with four measurements for one garment you have made, and a tolerance for each.
Inspect the garment in daylight in the 12-point order and measure it.
Mark each point pass or fail, and classify any fault as critical, major or minor.
activity.evidence: Completed checklist and spec sheet with pass or fail for each point

lessons.title: Finding the root cause of faults and correcting them
objectives: Trace common finishing faults to their real cause
Choose between repairing, remaking a part, or remaking the garment
Keep a simple fault log and find your most frequent faults
Change your method so the same fault does not return

blocks.text: Fixing a fault on one garment is important. Fixing the **reason** it happened is what makes you better. A puckered seam fixed by unpicking and resewing will return on the next garment if the real cause, wrong tension or a blunt needle, is still there. This lesson teaches you to ask "why" until you reach a cause you can change.

blocks.name: fixing-bugs
blocks.alt: A person fixing problems on a board
blocks.caption: Every fault has a cause; find it, fix it and change the method so it does not return.

blocks.text: Common faults, causes and fixes

head: Fault
Likely causes
Correction
Prevention
rows: Puckered seam
Tension too tight, blunt or wrong needle, fabric pulled while sewing
Unpick, change needle, adjust tension on scrap, resew
New needle every garment or two on fine fabric; test seam first
Skipped stitches
Wrong needle type (for example universal on knit), bent needle
Change to ballpoint or stretch needle; resew affected section
Match needle to fabric and replace bent needles
Wavy hem on knit
Fabric stretched under the foot
Unpick, steam to shrink back, resew with less pressure or walking foot
Stabilise hem with fusible tape; reduce foot pressure
Uneven collar points
Stitching guessed, not marked
Remake the collar if difference is visible
Use a stitching template
Lining pulling
Not enough ease, or lining shrank
Let out lining seams or rehem lining
Add ease; pre-shrink lining
Press shine
Iron too hot or no press cloth
Steam lightly through a damp cloth; may not fully disappear
Test heat on scrap, always use a press cloth on dark fabric

blocks.text: The five whys

A simple way to find the root cause is to keep asking "why". Stop when you reach something you can change in your method, your tools or your training. Write the answer down, because the point is to change what you do next time.

blocks.title: From fault to prevention
items: Spot the fault
Ask why, repeatedly
Find a changeable cause
Correct the garment
Change the method
blocks.caption: Correcting the garment fixes today; changing the method fixes every garment after it.

blocks.title: Worked example: the five whys on a fault log
blocks.context: For example, Hauwa in Kaduna runs a small workroom with two apprentices. She keeps a fault log for one month of 40 garments and counts the faults found at inspection.
steps: Her log shows: puckered seams 14, untrimmed threads 9, uneven hems 6, loose buttons 3, others 4. Total: 36 faults.
Puckered seams are 14 out of 36, about 39 percent, the biggest single problem.
Why puckered? Most are on one machine. Why that machine? Its needle has not been changed for weeks. Why not? No one is responsible for changing needles.
Root cause: no routine for needle changes. Action: a new needle at the start of every new fabric type, written on a card on the machine, checked by Hauwa each Monday.
The next month, she logs again: puckered seams drop to 4.
blocks.result: One small routine removed most of her biggest fault, and the fault log proved it worked.

blocks.text: Repair, remake a part, or remake the garment?

items: **Repair** when the fault can be undone without marks: a hem, a button, a short seam section.
**Remake the part** when unpicking will leave visible needle holes or stretching: a collar, a cuff, a waistband. Most of these are small pieces, so recutting costs little fabric.
**Remake the garment** only when the main fabric is damaged or the fit is wrong in a way that alterations cannot fix. Tell the client honestly and agree a new date.
On delicate fabrics such as satin, silk and some crepes, needle holes can stay visible after unpicking. Test on a scrap before deciding to repair.

blocks.title: Honesty with clients
blocks.text: If a fault means you will deliver late, tell the client as soon as you know, explain what you are fixing and give a new time you can keep. Clients forgive a delay that is explained; they rarely forgive a faulty garment delivered on time.
Keep your fault log simple: date, garment, fault, cause, action. Ten minutes at the end of each week to count the faults shows you exactly what to train apprentices on and which tool needs attention.
Machine checks that prevent many faults

items: Clean lint from under the needle plate and around the bobbin case at the end of each working day, using a small brush. Lint build-up causes skipped stitches and uneven tension.
Oil the machine only where and how often the manual says. Too much oil stains fabric; sew a few lines on scrap after oiling.
Rethread top and bobbin completely when stitches look wrong, with the presser foot raised so the thread sits between the tension discs.
Keep a fabric test strip by each machine and sew a short line before starting any new fabric.

blocks.text: When you train an apprentice, show her the fault log and ask her to inspect one of her own garments with the checklist before you do. People learn quickly when they find their own faults, and they start to prevent them rather than waiting to be corrected.

takeaways: Correcting a garment fixes one fault; changing the method prevents it
Ask why until you reach a cause you can change
A fault log shows your most frequent problem
Decide repair, remake part or remake garment by what unpicking will leave

activity.title: Start a fault log
steps: Create a log with columns: date, garment, fault, cause, action.
Inspect the last five garments you made or repaired and log every fault.
Count the faults by type and find the most frequent one.
Apply the five whys to that fault and write one change to your method.
activity.evidence: Fault log for five garments with counts and a written root cause and action

lessons.title: Final pressing, care labels and a professional handover
objectives: Do a final press suited to each fabric without shine or marks
Write a care card using the standard care symbols correctly
Package and hand over a garment so it arrives crease-free
Follow up after delivery and handle alteration requests fairly

blocks.text: The last hour of a job decides how the client feels about the whole garment. A crisp final press, a clear care card, careful packaging and a short, warm handover make your work look and feel like it came from a boutique. They also reduce complaints, because the client knows how to look after the garment.

blocks.name: order-delivered
blocks.alt: A person receiving a delivered package
blocks.caption: The handover is part of the product: packaging and care instructions travel with the garment.

blocks.text: The final press

items: Check the fibre and test the iron temperature on a scrap or a hidden seam allowance.
Press inside out where possible, and always through a press cloth on dark, shiny, embellished or synthetic fabrics.
Use a tailor's ham (a firm, rounded pressing cushion) for curved areas such as bust darts, sleeve caps and collars. A rolled-up towel can work if you do not have one.
Press, lift and move. Do not drag the iron across bias areas or hems.
Hang the garment immediately on a suitable hanger and let it cool and dry completely before packing.

blocks.text: Care symbols

Care symbols are set out in the international standard ISO 3758, and the GINETEX care labelling system is based on it. There are **five basic symbols**. Use them on a care card even if the garment has no sewn-in label.

head: Symbol
Meaning
How to read it
rows: Washtub
Washing
A number inside is the maximum water temperature in degrees Celsius; a hand in the tub means hand wash; a cross means do not wash
Triangle
Bleaching
Empty triangle: any bleach; triangle with two diagonal lines: only non-chlorine bleach; crossed: do not bleach
Square
Drying
A circle inside the square means tumble drying; lines inside mean natural drying such as line or flat drying
Iron
Ironing
One dot: low, up to about 110 degrees C; two dots: medium, up to about 150 degrees C; three dots: high, up to about 200 degrees C
Circle
Professional cleaning
Letters inside tell the dry cleaner which process to use; crossed means do not dry clean

blocks.title: Worked example: a care card for a beaded lace blouse
blocks.context: For example, Ijeoma in Asaba is handing over a beaded lace blouse with a polyester lining and an invisible zip.
steps: Washing: hand wash in cool water (washtub with a hand), because beads and lace are delicate.
Bleach: do not bleach (crossed triangle).
Drying: dry flat in the shade, not wrung (square with one horizontal line).
Ironing: low heat, one dot, from the inside only, never on the beads.
She adds: "Close the zip before washing. Store on a padded hanger." and her business name and WhatsApp number.
blocks.result: The client gets a clear card that protects the beading and lining, and has the maker's contact every time she opens her wardrobe.

blocks.text: Packaging and handover

items: Hang garments on a hanger that fits the shoulders; fold only knits that could stretch on a hanger.
Cover with a clear or branded garment bag. Put tissue paper inside sleeves and bodices for delivery so they arrive crease-free.
Attach the care card, a spare button if the garment has buttons, and a small piece of spare fabric for future repairs if available.
At handover, ask the client to try the garment on if she can, and show her the zip, the closures and the care card.
Confirm payment of the balance through a channel you can check, such as a bank transfer that has actually arrived in your account. Do not release the garment on a screenshot alone.

blocks.title: From last stitch to follow-up
items: Final inspection
Final press and cool
Care card and packing
Handover and fitting
Follow-up message
blocks.caption: Each step happens in this order so the garment leaves clean, pressed and documented.

blocks.title: Payment screenshots
blocks.text: Fake transfer screenshots and fake bank alert messages are a known scam. Check your own banking app or bank statement for the credit before handing over the garment. A real customer will understand a one-minute check.
Follow-up and alterations

Send a short message a few days after delivery to ask whether the garment fits and feels right, and ask for a photo if she is happy to share. Agree your alteration policy in advance and write it on the order card or receipt, for example: small adjustments free within a stated number of days, with the garment unwashed and unaltered by anyone else. A clear policy keeps both of you calm if something needs adjusting.

Before the garment leaves, take two or three clear photos of it on a hanger or form in daylight: front, back and one close-up of a finishing detail. These photos are your record that it left in good condition, and, with the client's permission, they become portfolio and WhatsApp status content. Never post a photo of the client herself without asking first.

blocks.title: Keep a small handover stock
blocks.text: Keep a box with hangers, garment bags, tissue paper, blank care cards and small envelopes for spare buttons. When the stock is ready, a careful handover takes only a few extra minutes per garment.

takeaways: Test heat, use a press cloth and let garments cool before packing
Use the five ISO 3758 care symbols on a care card
Pack with tissue, a spare button and the care card
Confirm payment in your own banking app before handover

activity.title: Handover kit
steps: Write a care card for one garment using at least four of the five care symbols.
Add your business name, contact and one special care instruction.
Pack the garment as for delivery with tissue paper and a garment bag.
Write the follow-up message you will send three days after delivery.

quiz.q: A spec sheet allows plus or minus 1 cm. A dress waist measures 40.2 cm flat and should be 82 cm. What is the result?
options: Pass: flat measurement is always used directly
quiz.explain: Double the flat measurement: 40.2 x 2 = 80.4 cm. That is 1.6 cm under 82 cm, outside the 1 cm tolerance.

quiz.q: During inspection a maker finds a broken needle tip inside a child's dress seam. How should it be classified?
quiz.explain: Anything that makes a garment unsafe is critical and must never be accepted.

quiz.q: In a month, a workroom logs 50 faults, 20 of them uneven hems. What share is that?
quiz.explain: 20 divided by 50 is 0.4, which is 40 percent, the biggest target for improvement.

quiz.q: Seams keep puckering on one machine. Which action fixes the root cause?
options: Unpick and resew each puckered seam
Set up a needle-change routine and test tension before each new fabric
Press the puckers flat with more heat
quiz.explain: Resewing fixes one garment. A routine for needles and tension removes the cause for every garment after.

quiz.q: On a care symbol, an iron with two dots means:
options: Medium heat, up to about 150 degrees C
High heat, up to about 200 degrees C
quiz.explain: In the ISO 3758 system, one dot is low, two dots medium (about 150 degrees C), three dots high.

quiz.q: A client sends a transfer screenshot and asks to collect her dress. What should the maker do?
options: Check her own bank app for the credit before releasing the dress
quiz.explain: Screenshots can be faked. Confirm the money has arrived in your own account first.

quiz.q: Unpicking a satin collar would leave visible needle holes. What is the best choice?
options: Hand it over as it is
quiz.explain: When unpicking leaves marks, remaking the small part is cheaper and cleaner than repairing or remaking everything.

finalQuiz.q: A client brings chiffon for a blouse with a slightly curved hem. Which hem is most suitable?
options: Narrow rolled hem of about 3 to 5 mm
finalQuiz.explain: Light, sheer fabric on a curve needs a narrow, light rolled hem; deep or interfaced hems would show and ripple.

finalQuiz.q: Why should a hem be marked up from the floor with the client in her shoes?
options: Bodies are not symmetrical and heel height changes the length, so the floor gives a level line
finalQuiz.explain: Measuring from the floor in the right shoes gives a hem that looks level when worn.

finalQuiz.q: A collar's under collar shows at the edge. What would have prevented this?
options: Trimming the under collar 2 to 3 mm smaller and understitching
Pressing from the right side only
finalQuiz.explain: A slightly smaller under collar and understitching make the seam roll under so it cannot be seen.

finalQuiz.q: A client's wrist is 17 cm. With 4 cm ease, 2 cm overlap and 1 cm seam allowances, what is the cut cuff length?
finalQuiz.explain: 17 + 4 + 2 = 23 cm finished, plus 1 + 1 cm seam allowances = 25 cm cut.

finalQuiz.q: A skirt waist is 80 cm. With 1.5 cm ease, 3 cm underlap and 1.5 cm seam allowances, what is the cut waistband length?
finalQuiz.explain: 80 + 1.5 + 3 = 84.5 cm finished, plus 3 cm of seam allowances = 87.5 cm.

finalQuiz.q: Before sewing an invisible zip, which step helps the needle sew right beside the coil?
options: Pressing the coil flat from the wrong side on a low heat
finalQuiz.explain: Pressing the coil away from the tape lets the invisible zip foot sew close, so the zip disappears into the seam.

finalQuiz.q: A button is 18 mm across and 3 mm thick. What is the starting buttonhole length?
finalQuiz.explain: Diameter plus thickness: 18 + 3 = 21 mm, then test on scrap.

finalQuiz.q: Where should a skirt lining be joined to the skirt at the hem?
options: Sewn to the skirt hem all round
Held at the side seams with short French tacks
finalQuiz.explain: French tacks keep the lining in place but let it move freely, and the two hems stay separate.

finalQuiz.q: Piping cord is 5 mm across and the seam allowance is 1.5 cm. About what bias strip width is needed?
finalQuiz.explain: Circumference is about 5 x 3.14 = 15.7 mm, about 1.6 cm. Add 1.5 + 1.5 cm: about 4.6 cm.

finalQuiz.q: A beaded test of 5 cm takes 25 minutes. At 1,200 naira an hour (approximate), what is the labour cost of 60 cm?
finalQuiz.explain: 60 / 5 = 12 sections x 25 minutes = 300 minutes = 5 hours. 5 x 1,200 = 6,000 naira.

finalQuiz.q: During inspection, a zip sticks halfway. How should this fault be classified and handled?
options: Minor: hand over and mention it
Not a fault if the zip closes eventually
finalQuiz.explain: A sticking zip makes the garment fail in use, so it is a major fault that must be corrected before handover.

finalQuiz.q: Which care symbol tells the client the maximum washing temperature?
options: A washtub with a number inside
finalQuiz.explain: In ISO 3758 care labelling, the washtub symbol shows washing, and the number inside is the maximum water temperature in degrees Celsius.

capstone.title: Boutique-standard finished garment and quality file
capstone.brief: Make or fully finish one garment that uses at least four techniques from this course (for example a blind hem, a stand collar or cuffs, an invisible zip and a lining or binding), inspect it with your written system, correct any faults and hand it over with a care card.
steps: Choose the garment and write an order card: client or wearer, fabric, style, finishes chosen for hem, collar or neckline, closure and lining or detail, with reasons.
Write a spec sheet with at least five finished measurements and a tolerance for each.
Sew the garment, photographing each finishing stage: hem, collar or cuffs, zip or buttons, lining, binding or embellishment.
Inspect it with the 12-point checklist in daylight, measure it against the spec sheet and classify every fault found.
Correct each fault, record its root cause and one change to your method in your fault log.
Do the final press, write a care card with the ISO 3758 symbols, pack it and hand it over, then send a follow-up message.
evidence: Order card with finishing choices and reasons
Spec sheet with measured results and pass or fail
Stage photos of each finishing technique
Fault log entries with root cause and method change
Photo of the pressed, packed garment with its care card
Text of the follow-up message and any feedback received
